extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate communicators, advertisers, and students of PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for the role, methods, ethics, and practices of a public relations (propaganda) counsel: how to analyze clients and publics, plan and execute campaigns using mass-psychology, coordinate with media/advertising, and maintain professional ethics and vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate public desire into organized action
rubrics_metrics.description: A desire for a specific reform, however widespread, cannot be translated into action until it is made articulate, organized, made vocal, and concentrated upon the proper law-making bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda is called upon to organize half-expressed demands so they will produce desired results; individual desires must be aggregated and focused on legislature or Congress to effect change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of propaganda by intelligent minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligent minorities need to make use of propaganda continuously and systematically to bring new ideas to public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress and development lie in active proselytizing minorities where selfish and public interests coincide; small groups can lead the majority via systematic propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role definition of public relations counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel interprets enterprises and ideas to the public and the public to promulgators of new enterprises and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He is concerned with courses of action, doctrines, systems and the securing of public support for them, and with tangible products and large trade groups; his function is analogous to a lawyer's but focused on public contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive client analysis before campaigning
rubrics_metrics.description: First efforts are devoted to analyzing the client's problems and making sure what he has to offer the public is something which the public accepts or can be brought to accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the product, the markets, the way the public reacts to the product, the attitude of the employees to the public and towards the product, and the cooperation of distribution agencies; avoid promoting a fundamentally unsound idea or product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify client practices to fit public expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: After analysis, shape the actions of the client so they will gain the interest, approval and acceptance of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise institutional or product modifications (examples: reorganize an orphan asylum on the 'cottage plan'; recommend a fast train to add prestige) rather than attempting to sell an inherently unacceptable product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the public by groups and leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the groups which must be reached and the leaders through whom those groups may be approached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment public into social, economic, geographical, age, doctrinal, language, cultural groups; identify and approach group leaders who influence these constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate client policies before public action
rubrics_metrics.description: Only after the double analysis of client and public and the collation of results should policies governing the client's practice, procedure and public habits be formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies agreed upon form the basis for subsequent propaganda steps; sometimes the counsel's work ends once policies are set, other cases require ongoing effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use varied means of communication appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: The means by which the public is apprised of the client's actions include conversation, letters, the stage, motion picture, radio, lecture platform, magazine, and daily newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations is not advertising but recommends advertising where indicated; coordinate with advertising agencies to supplement rather than duplicate efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous and frank information where required
rubrics_metrics.description: In many instances only a careful system of constant, thorough and frank information will make the public understand and appreciate value of what a client is doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain continuous efforts when necessary to preserve public understanding; lack of information or secrecy can breed suspicion with large consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain constant vigilance against rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel on public relations must maintain constant vigilance because inadequate information, or false information from unknown sources, may have results of enormous importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deal effectively with rumors and suspicions by attempting to stop their source, counteracting them promptly with correct or more complete information through the most effective channels, or establishing relations of confidence in the concern's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of new or unsuspected markets
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel's function may include the discovery of new markets, the existence of which had been unsuspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through analysis of client and public, identify unmet or latent demands and opportunities for expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic ideal of the profession
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of the profession is to make the producer understand what the public wants and to make the public understand the objectives of the producer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to eliminate waste and friction when industry does things the public does not want or when the public does not understand what is offered; foster mutual understanding between various social actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics: refuse dishonest, fraudulent, or antisocial clients
rubrics_metrics.description: While recognizing the right to present a case in its best light, the public relations counsel refuses a client whom he believes to be dishonest, a product which he believes to be fraudulent, or a cause which he believes to be antisocial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical restraints stem from professional conditions: the counsel is identified with his client in the public mind and must preserve professional credibility and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid client conflicts and hopeless cases
rubrics_metrics.description: He does not accept a client whose interests conflict with those of another client, whose case he believes to be hopeless, or whose product he believes to be unmarketable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen client engagements for conflicts of interest and realistic chances of success; decline engagements likely to damage reputation or be futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and not deceiving the public
rubrics_metrics.description: He should be candid in his dealings. His business is not to fool or hoodwink the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive secrecy or deception damages professional usefulness; maintain frankness in communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label propaganda material as to source
rubrics_metrics.description: When sending out propaganda material, it is clearly labeled as to source; the editor knows from whom it comes and what its purpose is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent sourcing allows editors to accept or reject material on merits as news and preserves credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and observe a professional ethical code
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession is developing an ethical code comparable to legal and medical professions, partly forced by the conditions of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics include client selection, candor, conflict avoidance, and refusal of fraudulent causes; operate in ways that sustain public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base propaganda on study of mass psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda seeks to base its operations upon definite knowledge drawn from direct observation of the group mind and application of consistent principles demonstrated by studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scientific methods—clipping services, scouts, personal study—to understand group motives, leaders, cliches, and impulses; accept that exact scientific accuracy is impossible and allow for margin of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence leaders to influence masses
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can influence the leaders, with or without their conscious cooperation, you automatically influence the group which they sway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize leader-oriented tactics because groups often follow trusted leaders; use trusted professionals (e.g., physicians) to change public habits rather than mass exhortation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and target true motives, not stated reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful propagandist must understand the true motives and not be content to accept the reasons which men give for what they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize unconscious desires, social symbols, compensatory substitutions (Freudian insight) and design messages that speak to underlying motives rather than surface rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit cliches and slogans to trigger group responses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the herd must think for itself it does so by means of cliches, pat words or images which stand for a whole group of ideas or experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playing upon an old cliche or manipulating a new one can swing mass emotions; use naming and labeling strategically (example: renaming 'hospitals' to 'evacuation posts' changed public reaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances to change customs and demand
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern propagandist creates circumstances which will modify public custom, thereby producing purchaser demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to sell pianos, develop acceptance of a home music room via exhibitions, staging events, inviting key influencers (violinist, artist, society leader) to create prestige and lift ideas into public taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from direct individual appeals to group-based influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of assaulting sales resistance by direct attack on individuals, the new salesmanship deals with men in the mass through their group formations to set up psychological and emotional currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move beyond repetitive, direct exhortations; design group-level interventions (events, influencers, institutional endorsements) that alter collective preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept limits: expect margins of error in mass psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific accuracy of results is not to be expected because many elements are beyond the propagandist's control; there must always be a wide margin of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for unpredictable events that can overshadow campaigns; use probabilistic reasoning rather than promises of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with advertising, but do not duplicate
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel on public relations is not an advertising man but he advocates advertising where indicated and often supplements advertising agency work without conflict or duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate PR and advertising strategically: call in PR counsel to complement advertising efforts, ensuring distinct roles and avoiding redundancy.
